props.title: Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker's Apocalypse

sections.content: Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker's Apocalypse (1991) stands as the definitive documentary about filmmaking chaos. Shot by Eleanor Coppola during the infamously troubled production of Apocalypse Now (1979), it captures Francis Ford Coppola's descent into near-madness as his Vietnam War epic spirals out of control. The documentary reveals Martin Sheen's on-set heart attack, Marlon Brando showing up overweight and unprepared, and a typhoon destroying expensive sets. It's the ultimate "making-of" film that surpasses mere behind-the-scenes footage to become a haunting parallel to the story of Kurtz's obsession in both Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness and Apocalypse Now itself.

sections.content: The tradition of documenting troubled productions reveals the thin line between artistic vision and megalomaniacal obsession. Lost in La Mancha (2002) shows Terry Gilliam's Don Quixote project crumbling under flash floods, NATO aircraft noise, and an injured leading actor. Burden of Dreams (1982) captures Werner Herzog's manic determination to haul a 320-ton steamship over a mountain in Peru - a feat many considered impossible but Herzog insisted on doing for real, not with special effects. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Making-Of Documentaries

While modern behind-the-scenes features often feel sanitized for marketing purposes, the raw honesty of Hearts of Darkness (1991) inspired a wave of unflinching production documentaries. Full Tilt Boogie (1997) exposed the grueling conditions on Robert Rodriguez's From Dusk Till Dawn (1996), while The Death of "Superman Lives": What Happened? (2015) detailed Tim Burton's failed Nicolas Cage Superman project through candid interviews and never-before-seen test footage. These films reveal the fascinating intersection of art, commerce, and human endurance.
